questions.prompt: Complete the sentence: "Every child ___ the right to education."
questions.explanation: Every child means one child, that is he or she, and with he, she or it the verb becomes has: every child has the right to education. The form "have" goes with I, you, we and they, "having" cannot be the verb of the sentence on its own, and "is" would need another structure altogether.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence: "Yesterday, we ___ the classroom for Teacher's Day."
questions.explanation: Yesterday is a finished moment, so the verb goes to the simple past, and decorate is regular: it already ends in e, so it takes only -d. The forms "decorate" and "decorates" are the present, and "will decorate" sends the action to the future, which yesterday forbids.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence: "Last Sunday, my father ___ a necklace for my mother."
questions.explanation: Last Sunday is over, and buy is an irregular verb: its simple past is bought. The forms "buy" and "buys" stay in the present, and "buyed" adds the regular -ed ending to a verb that refuses it.

questions.prompt: Complete both blanks: "The clown ___ very funny and the children ___ excited."
questions.explanation: One clown is he, and I, he, she and it take was; several children are they, and you, we and they take were. So the pair is was for the clown and were for the children, and the three other pairs give at least one of the two subjects the form of the other.

questions.prompt: In which of these past verbs does the final -ed add a whole new syllable, the sound /ɪd/?
questions.explanation: The verb wait already ends in the sound t, and nothing can be glued to a t, so a whole little syllable appears: wait-ed. In talked the ending is the quiet /t/, and in played and hugged it is the /d/ that shakes your throat, and none of the three adds a syllable.
